item.title: Kairos Extortion, North Korean PolinRider Packages, and EPS Supplier Phishing
item.content:encoded:
North Korean Hackers Publish 108 Malicious Packages and Extensions in PolinRider Campaign — Must Read

North Korea-linked Contagious Interview actors are actively spreading the PolinRider supply-chain campaign through 108 malicious npm, Composer, Go, and Chrome packages/extensions, using compromised maintainer access and developer tooling to infect repositories. Developers who installed affected packages should assume compromise, rotate secrets from a clean machine, and audit repositories for hidden VS Code tasks and suspicious config-file changes.

  • North Korean threat actors linked to the Contagious Interview campaign have published 108 unique malicious packages and web browser extensions across npm, Packagist, Go, and Google Chrome as part of the active PolinRider campaign.
  • Socket reported that the 162 malicious release artifacts include 19 npm libraries, 10 Composer packages, 61 Go modules, and one Google Chrome extension.
  • PolinRider has compromised 1,951 public GitHub repositories associated with 1,047 unique owners as of April 11, 2026, and has merged with the TaskJacker cluster that adds malicious VS Code task files to repositories.
  • The malware searches infected computers for configuration files such as postcss.config.mjs, tailwind.config.js, eslint.config.mjs, next.config.mjs, babel.config.js, and app.js, then appends malicious JavaScript code to them.
  • The latest payload reaches out to TRON, Aptos, and BNB Smart Chain services to fetch an encrypted second-stage payload that unpacks to DEV#POPPER RAT and OmniStealer.

U.S. Government Entity Paid Kairos $1 Million in Data-Theft Extortion Case — Should Read

A U.S. government entity believed to be Union County, Ohio paid Kairos about $1 million after attackers stole sensitive data and threatened to leak it, despite no evidence of file encryption. The case highlights the shift from traditional ransomware to pure data-theft extortion, where paying offers no real proof stolen files were deleted.

  • A U.S. government entity paid about $1 million to Kairos to prevent stolen files from being leaked, according to a Ransom-ISAC case study based on a leaked negotiation chat and blockchain tracing.
  • Rakesh Krishnan did not name the victim, but evidence in the chat points to Union County, Ohio, which reported a May 2025 cyber incident affecting 45,487 residents and staff.
  • Krishnan found no sign that Kairos encrypted any machines, used a locker, or demanded payment for a decryption key; the threat was to publish stolen data.
  • The negotiation lasted about a month, with Kairos lowering its demand from $3 million to a final $1 million payment made on June 13, 2025.
  • The payment was about 9.44 bitcoin and was later split and moved through wallets toward deposit addresses tied to Bybit, OKX, and BELQI.

The File Format Your Gateway Forgot: EPS Macros Hidden in a Logo ZIP — Should Read

A real supplier’s DKIM-passing email delivered a logo ZIP that looked harmless but contained EPS vector files with macro-like code, exposing a blind spot in gateways that don’t deeply parse programmable file formats. The key lesson is that authenticated senders and clean first-pass scans are not enough when compromised vendors can send unusual attachment types hidden inside legitimate-looking archives.

  • A marine manufacturing company received an Italian email from a known supplier with a ZIP attachment named Logo nuovo.zip that appeared to contain new company logo materials.
  • A first-pass attachment scan marked the ZIP as clean, but deeper content analysis unpacked it and rated it CRITICAL with a 0.90 score.
  • The archive contained a brand-manual PDF and two EPS vector files that were flagged for VBA-like or macro-like strings, while the DOCX files had no macro hits and a PNG signature image was judged low risk.
  • The article explains that EPS is a programmable PostScript format that email gateways may treat like a simple image and fail to parse deeply.
  • The message passed DKIM from the supplier’s real domain but had no SPF record and no DMARC policy, and the article describes this as likely vendor email compromise.
